messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At eighty, Nneka’s memories still pull her back to the military transport bus she fled sixty years prior. The vehicle was packed with trembling families, its metal interior vibrating as soldiers swept through the rows. She remembered the glint of rifles and batons pressed against her ribs, the way she was shoved forward with sudden, unpredictable motions that taught her body to live in permanent defense. In that confined space, stripped of her name and reduced to a numbered bundle of bones, she felt utterly stripped of her personhood. That specific moment on that specific bus explains why, decades later, the screech of city bus brakes or the metallic flash of a street vendor’s knife still drops her stomach into her shoes. When the brakes shriek outside her church parish, Nneka’s hands immediately clamp onto the pew, her eyes darting to the aisle to watch every stranger for signs of hostility. Her head twitches forward, then snaps back to check behind her, certain that the men who hunted her are always three steps out. The sight of a bus or a weapon instantly drives her to pull her high-collared coat tighter and refuse to speak about what it reminds her of. That same visual cue drops her straight into a state of hypervigilance. The metallic flash of a weapon or the rattling of a bus door only reinforces her quiet, unshakable conviction that what happened to her was deeply unjust and that justice has never come. As the years passed in exile, the memories refused to stay buried. They forced their way into her mind during morning prayers, accompanied by the crackle of radio static and the guttural shouts she had heard during the escape. The accounts felt so extreme that Nneka sometimes caught herself whispering that the story couldn’t possibly be true, that it had to be a dream she was mistaking for her own life. Yet, because she is certain that dwelling on that injustice will cause her to break down completely, she enforces a strict rule against talking about the past, hiding her body in layers of clothing, and fleeing from medical offices before a doctor can ask questions. By refusing to process the trauma or seek help, she starves her mind of the chance to heal; the memories only grow heavier and more uncontrolled. Each time the auditory echoes return, they convince her that the event is too horrific to be real, yet they also prove beyond doubt that she was treated as a mere object. That same bitterness about the past unfairness acts like a key in a lock, forcing the intrusive memories back into her mind the moment she tries to look away. The conviction that life was fundamentally unjust makes the ordinary screech of a bus brake feel like a fresh wound, while her lingering belief that she was abandoned by any fair tribunal sharpens her suspicion. She reads every glance as a prelude to violence and lives as though her life is perpetually under siege. Constantly scanning for danger and checking behind her on every street corner pulls the auditory echoes of the escape right into the present. That relentless vigilance confirms her worst fears, deepening her sense that the world is irredeemably unjust. Her habit of concealing herself and shutting down conversation ensures that ordinary triggers are never neutralized, so a simple ride across town instantly reignites the panic. Staying silent and hidden means she never learns that people are safe, so every sudden movement by a deacon or a parishioner still jolts her into immediate defense. The cycle tightened with each passing season. Avoiding the doctors and withholding her story meant the memories never faded; they only grew heavier, pushing her further into the belief that life had been a profound injustice and that she was stripped of her humanity. That bitter appraisal, in turn, sharpened her threat monitoring, making her read every glance as a prelude to harm. The monitoring itself pulled the old memories back into the present, and the memories only proved that seeking help was too dangerous. Now, after her husband of forty-two years fell ill and needed her to navigate the healthcare system, Nneka found herself trapped between a crumbling marriage and a paralyzing dread. She finally booked an appointment, terrified that the therapy room would unlock the door she had spent decades keeping shut, yet desperately hoping someone might finally believe that what happened to her was real.
